analysis.one_liner: Caps military spending and cancels major weapons programs to cut defense budgets by tens of billions a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House National Security Committee and died there at the end of the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have put a hard ceiling on total military spending — $245 billion in fiscal 1997, dropping by $10 billion a year to $210 billion by 2001. To get there, it would have canceled or slashed specific programs: no more Seawolf submarines, Trident II nuclear missiles, B-2 bombers beyond the 20 already planned, a new aircraft carrier, C-17 cargo planes, MILSTAR satellites, or an anti-satellite weapons program, plus deep cuts to missile defense research, the F-22 fighter, and Energy Department nuclear weapons work. It also would have ended federal subsidies that help U.S. companies sell weapons abroad, and required any remaining savings to come from consolidating bases and laboratories.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would have kept tens of billions of dollars a year that the bill redirected away from weapons procurement, missile defense research, and nuclear weapons programs — money that could go toward deficit reduction or other priorities. Communities near DOE nuclear facilities would also have gained, since the bill requires full funding for environmental cleanup there.

how_it_helps.text: Caps total military spending at $245 billion for fiscal 1997, falling by $10 billion a year to $210 billion by fiscal 2001, freeing those tax dollars for other uses or deficit reduction.

Terminates specific expensive weapons programs: additional Seawolf submarines, Trident II D-5 nuclear missiles, the new aircraft carrier, MILSTAR satellites, the C-17 cargo aircraft, and the anti-satellite weapons program, and slashes spending on the F-22 fighter and the new attack submarine to a fraction of fiscal 1996 levels.

Caps ballistic missile defense research at $1.25 billion a year and cuts Energy Department nuclear weapons work roughly in half, cancels the tritium production program and the National Ignition Facility, and ends federal subsidies that market and finance conventional arms sales to foreign nations.
Requires adequate funding for environmental cleanup and waste management at nuclear weapons facilities, and requires funds for defense community and worker transition when bases close.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and their employees (shipbuilders, aircraft makers, nuclear weapons labs), and the communities that depend on those jobs and bases; also members of Congress and constituents who value those weapons programs for national security or local employment.

drawbacks.text: Cancelling the C-17 cargo aircraft and the new aircraft carrier would have cut capability that even some defense reformers considered worth keeping, and cancellation of partially built programs incurs termination costs the bill itself acknowledges by carving out contract termination expenses.

Reaching the spending caps would have required cuts to the active-duty force and consolidation of bases and laboratories, which would cost jobs in defense-dependent communities, although the bill requires transition aid and directs that cuts not harm readiness or the quality of life of remaining forces.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary taxpayers, the benefits were large and the costs modest: the bill would have redirected tens of billions from weapons programs toward deficit reduction or other priorities, while cutting Cold War-era weapons programs the Cold War no longer justified. The main genuine costs were to communities and workers dependent on defense bases, labs, and production lines — the bill acknowledged this with transition funding requirements — and a plausible argument that some programs it cut (C-17 cargo aircraft, for example) had real military value. On the whole, the bill's benefits to the general public exceeded its costs, though its across-the-board approach was blunter than a program-by-program review would be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House National Security Committee the day it was introduced, never received a vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Representative Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on March 29, 1996, and it was referred to the House Committee on National Security the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
Its 11 cosponsors were all Democrats or the Independent, and no member of the majority leadership took it up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors and the weapons programs they depend on kept their funding, and taxpayers continued paying for programs the bill would have canceled.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

for.name: 10 of 435 House members plus one Independent cosponsor

against.name: House leadership and National Security Committee majority (104th Congress)
against.role: House Republican majority controlling the committee and floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or vote; it remained in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; the Republican majority that controlled the National Security Committee never acted on it, so the bill stalled along partisan lines without a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill terminates or sharply cuts many of their largest programs — B-2 bombers, Seawolf submarines, Trident II missiles, a new aircraft carrier, C-17 cargo planes, F-22 fighters, MILSTAR satellites — ending billions in annual revenue. Ordinary taxpayers bear those costs instead when such programs proceed.

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons complex and national laboratories
industries.note: Cancels tritium production and the National Ignition Facility, halves stockpile stewardship spending, and mandates consolidation of DOE and NASA laboratories, cutting the nuclear weapons establishment's budget roughly in half.
Ends Defense Department funds that subsidize the marketing and financing of American weapon sales abroad, removing a public subsidy for the arms trade.
